title: EU enlargement: Could new members face 15 years of oversight?
content:
The European Commission has presented MEPs with proposals to prepare the EU for a larger membership. The package sets out five areas for reform, from limiting national veto powers and expanding gradual integration to introducing safeguards designed to “hit hard” against countries that breach EU rules after joining. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos argues that new members will not weaken the bloc but help make it fit for the future.

Presenting the Commission’s enlargement package in Strasbourg on 6 October, Kos described it as an “insurance policy” against democratic backsliding following enlargement. The package proposes a time-limited system of safeguards that would subject new member states to special oversight for up to 15 years after accession.

In cases of serious breaches of EU values, the mechanism could allow a country’s voting rights in the Council of the EU to be suspended. Kos said such protections were necessary to “protect ourselves”, pointing to “lessons from previous enlargements”.

For Kos, enlargement is not simply about bringing more countries into the EU. It is also an opportunity to make the Union stronger, more flexible and better equipped to take decisions.

title: Will the UK rejoin the EU? Andy Burnham’s plan has two goals, expert says
content:
Until recently, the British government was reluctant to entertain the possibility of rejoining the European Union. Now, London’s position appears to be shifting. At the Labour Party’s annual conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for a debate on the future of Britain’s relationship with the EU.

“Brexit has done more harm than good,” Burnham said. He outlined several possible paths forward: maintaining the current relationship, joining the EU customs union, returning to the single market or even becoming a full member of the bloc again. On the last option, he suggested Britain could go “all the way”.

Burnham has stressed, however, that rejoining the EU remains a distant prospect. He has also suggested that another referendum might not necessarily be required.

According to Krzysztof Winkler, an analyst at the Warsaw Enterprise Institute, a Polish economic policy think tank, the prime minister’s position reflects both economic and political considerations.

“Western societies are now deeply divided between liberal-left and conservative camps. Essentially, we’re dealing with two very different ways of looking at the world,” Winkler explains.

title: Planetary diet in Polish schools sparks controversy: “The biggest problem is parents”
content:
It all started with a single dish made from beans or lentils. Before long, Poland was embroiled in a heated debate over hungry schoolchildren, digestive problems and claims of forced veganism. The trigger? A new government regulation changing what can be served in school canteens.

But first, what exactly is the planetary diet? Despite claims circulating online, it is not a Polish government initiative designed to take meat off children’s menus.

The term planetary health diet gained international attention in 2019, when the EAT-Lancet Commission, an international group of scientists, proposed a way of eating that would be healthier for people and less damaging to the environment.

It is not a vegan diet. Although largely plant-based, it allows for animal products, including dairy, poultry and fish. The emphasis is on eating more vegetables, fruit, whole grains, nuts and legumes, while consuming less red meat and sugar.

Which brings us to Polish schools — and the legumes that have become an unlikely source of national controversy.

title: The Draft Notice: A Fake News Story That Resurfaces Every Year in Romania
content:
The image circulating online is fake. It claims to be a “Notice of Conscription” issued by the Ilfov County Military Centre, summoning a young man – apparently born after 2000, judging by the details visible on the document – to report on 20 October 2026 to complete the formalities for being “drafted into the Romanian Army”.

The Ministry of National Defence has stressed that the document is an attempt to mislead the public, with no legal basis and no connection to any actual developments.

The false claim has surfaced as the ministry is providing updates on MOBEX B-IF-26, an exercise to assess the mobilisation reserve currently taking place in Bucharest and Ilfov County.

“Mobile phone screens have recently been flooded with a purported Ministry of National Defence document claiming that a young man is being drafted into the army […] It is just another disinformation attempt,” acting Defence Minister Radu Miruță warned.

He urged the public to check information against official sources before sharing it.

title: Israel: How the October 7 massacre saved Netanyahu
content:
Karolina Zbytniewska, FocusEurope.pl: On the anniversary of the bloody October 7 and before the Knesset elections on October 27, what is the political mood in Israel?

Joel Schalit, theBattleground.eu: October 7 is treated as the beginning of a new era – our 9/11 moment. It seemed to confirm the right’s darkest vision of Israel’s place in the Middle East and Palestinian attitudes towards Israel and Jews: the narrative Benjamin Netanyahu and his people have promoted for years. 

Netanyahu presents it as a watershed in Jewish history worldwide, extending its significance beyond the attack on Israel itself.

Discontent with him has grown, but I don’t know whether it will be enough to remove him in the October 27 elections. He has shaped Israeli politics since the early 1990s and radically transformed the country for the worse.

And here a personal disclaimer: I am and will always be part of Israel. My family came from Kharkiv and Galați in Romania during the First Aliyah and has been in the region since the 1880s. However, politically, I have never been more disenchanted with the country or Netanyahu’s role in shaping it.

title: Slovakia’s Security Council meets amid growing security incidents – yet barely mentions Russia
content:
After a long wait, the government is quietly convening the Security Council, which will meet on 7 October. According to its published agenda and a source from government circles who spoke to euBrief, however, the meeting is not a response to the growing number of security incidents, but a routine session.

This fact is surprising because at the end of August, an act of sabotage targeting a drone factory was foiled in the eastern Slovak city of Prešov. Last Friday, German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung subsequently reported on a group linked to Russia’s military intelligence service GRU, which allegedly operated from Slovakia. The group was reportedly behind the attack in Prešov as well.

According to security expert Domicián Zahorjan of the NEST Institute, who previously worked at the Centre for Countering Hybrid Threats under the Interior Ministry, this amounts to a serious underestimation of the situation.

title: As Belarus plans a new unit at Astravyets NPP, experts do not mince their words: A catastrophe is possible
content:
Although Belarus’s 2025 national report presents the plant as very safe, experts are calling for independent international inspections and warn that an additional unit would increase not only the risk of possible accidents, but also the scale of long-term risks associated with radioactive waste and the environment, including the possibility of an environmental disaster.

The latest National Threat Assessment, cited by ELTA, notes that Belarus plans to build a third unit at the Astravyets Nuclear Power Plant alongside the two already in operation.

“Belarusian Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Karankevich publicly announced Belarus’s decision to build a third unit at the Astravyets Nuclear Power Plant site in November 2025. He also said that an assessment of the feasibility of building a new nuclear power plant in the Mogilev Region was continuing,” the intelligence services said.

title: Latvia election: Russia, drones and coalition uncertainty
content:
Latvia will elect 100 members of its unicameral parliament, the Saeima. The vote comes after a change of government. In May, Prime Minister Evika Siliņa of New Unity (Jaunā Vienotība, JV) resigned after the social democratic, left-wing and green Progressives withdrew from the governing coalition. At the heart of the dispute were the dismissal of Defence Minister Andris Sprūds and the way the government had responded to incidents involving drones violating Latvian airspace.

Parliament subsequently approved Andris Kulbergs as prime minister. He was backed by the United List (Latvian: Apvienotais saraksts, AS), a centre-right, green-conservative alliance formed ahead of the 2022 parliamentary election.

The latest SKDS poll, conducted between 4 and 16 September among more than 2,000 citizens, put Kulbergs’s United List in first place with 14.4% support. In second place was the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians (SV/AJ) alliance, which represents Russian-speaking voters, with 9.4%. The populist Latvia First (LPV) would also enter parliament with 9.2%, followed by the Progressives on 6.2% and the National Alliance on 5.6%.

title: 72 Hours or Two Weeks? Europe Takes Different Approaches to How Prepared People Should Be for a Crisis
content:
This raises the same practical question across Europe: how long should an individual household be able to cope on its own?

Some countries already have a clear answer – at least 72 hours. Others recommend being prepared for three to seven days, or even two weeks in certain scenarios. In some countries, there is no general preparedness timeframe at all.

The differences are not limited to the number of days. Countries also have different ideas about what preparedness actually means: in some, it means having water, food and medicines at home; elsewhere, it also includes alternative heating, cooking, electricity and communication, as well as access to civil protection infrastructure.

Three days have become something of a symbol of civil preparedness in Europe in recent years.

title: Has Russia deployed 80,000 troops near the Latvian and Estonian borders?
content:
Talk of possible mobilisation in Russia, together with reports that the aggressor state is preparing up to 20,000 beds in civilian hospitals near the Baltic Sea, has added to public concern. But public anxiety also creates fertile ground for false information.

In early September, a social media post claimed that Russia had deployed a “new army” of up to 80,000 troops near its borders with Latvia and Estonia, citing purported information from Lithuanian intelligence. The claim is false.

On 1 September this year, an anonymous account called “Кассандра” (Kassandra) published a post on Threads with an alarming introduction: “Don’t make any plans for autumn. We’re taking the Baltics. Lithuanian intelligence reports that the Baltic people are soon going to be ***.” The post claimed that Russian armed forces had moved hundreds of military trucks to the borders with Latvia and Estonia, that new offensive divisions had been formed from brigades stationed there, and that the total strength of this “new army” was between 50,000 and 80,000 troops.

The post also claimed that “fresh satellite images confirm the troop buildup. The concentration of equipment is alarming NATO and the Baltic people.”
